data.title: Nitra in the 9th century – a drawing of the central hillfort of the principality
data.excerpt: Our collaborator Tomáš Humaj has drawn his impression of the hillfort on the castle hill at Nitra, where the central hillfort of the Principality of Nitra most probably stood in the 9th century. The drawing shows only the defences of the castle hill itself, not the presumed fortification of the suburbium or the surrounding hillforts.
data.metaTitle: Nitra in the 9th century – the central hillfort drawn
data.metaDescription: Tomáš Humaj's drawing reconstructs the hillfort on Nitra castle hill in the 9th century – the centre of the Principality of Nitra – from plans and ramparts.

mediaTexts.alt: A drawing of a two-part hillfort with an acropolis on a promontory and an extensive bailey

children.text: Our collaborator Tomáš Humaj has drawn for us an impression of the presumed appearance of

on the castle hill, where the central hillfort of the Principality of Nitra most probably stood in the 9th century. The drawing records only the defences of the castle hill itself and does not include the presumed fortification of the suburbium, nor the surrounding hillforts.

In making the drawing we started from the plans known so far from archaeologists, which record the presumed course of the fortification of the castle hill, from reconstructions of the excavated parts of the Great Moravian rampart, whose remains survive in some places (the stone front revetment), from aerial photographs of the castle hill and from surviving copper engravings from the later Middle Ages. We have kept the presumed entrance to the hillfort in the western part of the castle hill and respected the configuration of the terrain and the present-day fortification on the acropolis of the castle, because in our view, given the terrain, it is highly probable that in the period of the Principality of Nitra too a defensive wall was built in this place, separating the highest part of the hillfort (the acropolis) from the bailey. On the acropolis of the hillfort archaeologists assume a stone palace building and, of course, a masonry church as well. In addition, several further prestigious buildings can be assumed within the enclosure of the acropolis, since the closest family members of the prince evidently lived here, and perhaps also other important dignitaries of the secular or ecclesiastical power. That is why the buildings on the acropolis are, for that period, very large and splendid. In the bailey we have placed several smaller log buildings, where craftsmen, merchants and members of the retinue could have lived. We did not opt for too dense a built-up area in the bailey, because even the oldest depictions of the castle suggest that there were not very many buildings here – evidently for reasons of defence.

It should be pointed out that this is evidently the very first attempt to draw the central hillfort of Nitra and that it is an amateur drawing of ours. If we have made mistakes in anything, they were unintentional, but we will gladly accept constructive criticism. Perhaps on the basis of such criticism, and of this first effort of ours, someone else will attempt to create a more accurate drawing, which we would also be very glad to publish.

Besides the depiction of the castle itself, we are also trying to create a more comprehensive view of the centre of Nitra in the period of the 9th century, which would record the fortified suburbium and the surrounding hillforts. Let us hope that this drawing too will turn out well.
Our great thanks go once again to the author.
